sectionTitle: Using the Earth's resources and obtaining potable water

specStatements.text: Humans use the Earth’s resources to provide warmth, shelter, food and transport.
Natural resources, supplemented by agriculture, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels.
Finite resources from the Earth, oceans and atmosphere are processed to provide energy and materials.

Chemistry plays an important role in improving agricultural and industrial processes to provide new products and in sustainable development, which is development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
Students should be able to:
state examples of natural products that are supplemented or replaced by agricultural and synthetic products
distinguish between finite and renewable resources given appropriate information.
Students should be able to:
extract and interpret information about resources from charts, graphs and tables
use orders of magnitude to evaluate the significance of data.

Water of appropriate quality is essential for life. For humans, drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes. Water that is safe to drink is called potable water. Potable water is not pure water in the chemical sense because it contains dissolved substances.
The methods used to produce potable water depend on available supplies of water and local conditions.
In the United Kingdom (UK), rain provides water with low levels of dissolved substances (fresh water) that collects in the ground and in lakes and rivers, and most potable water is produced by:
choosing an appropriate source of fresh water
passing the water through filter beds
sterilising.
Sterilising agents used for potable water include chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.

If supplies of fresh water are limited, desalination of salty water or sea water may be required. Desalination can be done by distillation or by processes that use membranes such as reverse osmosis. These processes require large amounts of energy.
Students should be able to:
distinguish between potable water and pure water
describe the differences in treatment of ground water and salty water
give reasons for the steps used to produce potable water.
Required practical 8: analysis and purification of water samples from different sources, including pH, dissolved solids and distillation.

Urban lifestyles and industrial processes produce large amounts of waste water that require treatment before being released into the environment. Sewage and agricultural waste water require removal of organic matter and harmful microbes. Industrial waste water may require removal of organic matter and harmful chemicals.
Sewage treatment includes:
screening and grit removal
sedimentation to produce sewage sludge and effluent
anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge
aerobic biological treatment of effluent.
Students should be able to comment on the relative ease of obtaining potable water from waste, ground and salt water.
The Earth’s resources of metal ores are limited.

Copper ores are becoming scarce and new ways of extracting copper from low-grade ores include phytomining, and bioleaching. These methods avoid traditional mining methods of digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.
Phytomining uses plants to absorb metal compounds. The plants are harvested and then burned to produce ash that contains metal compounds.
Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.
The metal compounds can be processed to obtain the metal. For example, copper can be obtained from solutions of copper compounds by displacement using scrap iron or by electrolysis.
Students should be able to evaluate alternative biological methods of metal extraction, given appropriate information.

scopeNotes.statement: Desalination can be done by distillation or by processes that use membranes such as reverse osmosis.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the two routes named in the specification are taught: distillation, and membrane processes of which reverse osmosis is the given example. Nothing is asked about osmotic pressure, membrane structure, operating pressures or the design of a desalination plant, because the specification names the processes and states only that they require large amounts of energy.

scopeNotes.statement: Sterilising agents used for potable water include chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only chlorine, ozone and ultraviolet light are taught as sterilising agents. No chlorination equations, dosing levels or disinfection by-products are introduced, and ultraviolet light is treated exactly as the specification treats it - as a sterilising agent, not as an added chemical.

scopeNotes.statement: new ways of extracting copper from low-grade ores include phytomining, and bioleaching
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only phytomining and bioleaching are taught as the alternative biological methods, and only for copper, which is the metal the specification names. No named plant or bacterial species, and no biochemistry of metal uptake, is required. All of this material is marked higher tier, as 4.10.1.4 is.

scopeNotes.statement: copper can be obtained from solutions of copper compounds by displacement using scrap iron or by electrolysis
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the two routes the specification gives are taught. Displacement is justified by the reactivity of iron compared with copper, and electrolysis is used only at the level of which electrode the copper forms at; half equations, purification of copper by electrolysis and electrode reactions in detail belong to 4.4 and are not taught here.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should be able to evaluate alternative biological methods of metal extraction, given appropriate information.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Evaluation is set up as the specification words it - given appropriate information. The one evaluation question supplies its own yield and waste-rock figures in the stem, so students judge from data rather than recalling a memorised list of advantages and disadvantages that the specification does not itself state.

concepts.definition: Anything taken from the Earth, the oceans or the atmosphere that people use. Humans use the Earth's resources to provide warmth, shelter, food and transport; natural resources, supplemented by agriculture, provide food, timber, clothing and fuels.

A resource that is being used up far faster than it is being formed, so supplies will eventually run out. Finite resources from the Earth, oceans and atmosphere are processed to provide energy and materials. Crude oil, natural gas and metal ores are finite.

A resource that is replaced at the same rate as, or faster than, it is used, so it can be maintained if it is managed. Timber from a replanted forest and wool from sheep are renewable. Being renewable does not mean supplies are unlimited if the rate of use is too high.

Development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. Chemistry contributes to it by improving agricultural and industrial processes and by providing new products.

A product obtained by farming, which supplements what can be gathered from the wild. Farmed crops and animals supply food, timber, clothing fibres such as cotton and wool, and fuels. Agricultural products are still natural products, not synthetic ones.

A man-made substitute for a natural product, made by chemical reactions from raw materials such as crude oil. Synthetic rubber can replace natural rubber from latex, and synthetic fibres can supplement cotton and wool for clothing.

A factor of ten. Two quantities differ by one order of magnitude if one is about ten times the other, and by two orders of magnitude if one is about a hundred times the other. Orders of magnitude are used to judge whether a difference in data is significant.

Water that is safe to drink. It must have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and of microbes. Potable water is not pure water in the chemical sense, because it still contains dissolved substances.

Water containing only water molecules, with no dissolved substances at all. Chemically pure water can be produced by distillation. Pure and potable are different ideas: potable water is safe to drink but is not chemically pure.

Water with low levels of dissolved substances. In the UK, rain provides fresh water that collects in the ground and in lakes and rivers, and this is the usual starting point for producing potable water.

Beds of sand and gravel that the chosen fresh water is passed through. They remove insoluble solids such as grit, leaves and suspended particles. They do not remove dissolved salts, and they are not relied on to make the water safe from microbes.
The step that kills microbes in the water so that it is safe to drink. It is carried out after filtering, and it does not remove any dissolved salts from the water.

The agents used for potable water include chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light. Chlorine and ozone are chemical agents added to the water; ultraviolet light kills microbes without adding anything to the water.

The removal of dissolved salts from salty water or sea water to make it potable. It is used where supplies of fresh water are limited. It can be done by distillation or by processes that use membranes such as reverse osmosis, and these processes require large amounts of energy.

Boiling water and condensing the vapour, so that the water collected has been separated from the dissolved solids left behind. It gives chemically pure water, and it is one of the two desalination routes; it requires large amounts of energy.

A desalination process that uses membranes: water is forced through a membrane that holds back the dissolved salts. It is the specification's example of a membrane process, and like distillation it requires large amounts of energy.

Fresh water that has collected in the ground, one of the UK sources of water with low levels of dissolved substances. It is treated by choosing the source, passing it through filter beds and sterilising it; it is not distilled.

Water with high levels of dissolved salts. It cannot be made potable by filtering and sterilising alone, because those steps do not remove dissolved salts; it must be desalinated. This is why the method used depends on the available supplies and local conditions.

Water produced in large amounts by urban lifestyles and industrial processes, which requires treatment before being released into the environment. Sewage and agricultural waste water require removal of organic matter and harmful microbes.

The sequence used on sewage before it is released: screening and grit removal, sedimentation to produce sewage sludge and effluent, anaerobic digestion of the sludge, and aerobic biological treatment of the effluent.
The first stage of sewage treatment, in which large solid objects and grit are removed from the incoming sewage. It is a physical separation and removes neither dissolved chemicals nor microbes.
The stage in which the screened sewage is left to settle. Solids sink to produce sewage sludge, and the liquid above it is the effluent. The two are then treated separately.
The treatment given to sewage sludge, in which microorganisms break down the organic matter in the absence of air. It is applied to the sludge, not to the effluent.

The treatment given to the effluent, in which air is supplied so that aerobic microorganisms break down the remaining organic matter and harmful microbes are dealt with. It is applied to the effluent, not to the sludge.

Waste water from industrial processes. As well as organic matter, it may require the removal of harmful chemicals, which is what distinguishes its treatment from that of sewage and agricultural waste water.
A rock containing enough of a metal compound to make extracting the metal worthwhile. The Earth's resources of metal ores are limited, and copper ores in particular are becoming scarce.
An ore that contains only a small percentage of the metal. As copper-rich ores run out, low-grade ores have to be used, and phytomining and bioleaching are new ways of extracting copper from them.
A method that uses plants to absorb metal compounds. The plants are harvested and then burned to produce ash that contains the metal compounds, which can then be processed to obtain the metal.

A method that uses bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds. Like phytomining, it avoids the traditional mining steps of digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.

The solution produced by the bacteria in bioleaching, which contains metal compounds dissolved out of the low-grade ore. It is not metal itself; the compounds in it still have to be processed to obtain the metal.

One way of obtaining copper from solutions of copper compounds. Iron is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper from the solution: Fe + CuSO4 goes to FeSO4 + Cu. Scrap iron is used because it is cheap.

The other way given for obtaining copper from solutions of copper compounds. Passing a current through the solution deposits copper at the negative electrode, because copper ions are positively charged.

Analysis and purification of water samples from different sources, including pH, dissolved solids and distillation. The pH is measured, the mass of dissolved solids is found by evaporating a known volume and weighing the residue, and distillation is used to purify the sample.

misconceptions.question: If water is safe to drink, does that make it pure water?
misconceptions.correct: Potable water is safe to drink but is not pure water in the chemical sense, because it contains dissolved substances.
misconceptions.misconception: Tap water must be pure, because it has been cleaned and it is safe to drink - pure and clean mean the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English 'pure' is used to mean clean, wholesome or unspoilt, and bottled water is even advertised as pure. Chemistry gives the word a much narrower meaning that students meet earlier in 4.1 and rarely connect to drinking water.
misconceptions.correction: In chemistry, pure means a single substance only. Evaporate tap water to dryness and a residue of dissolved salts is left, which proves it is a mixture. Potable means low enough levels of dissolved salts and microbes to be safe, which is a different test entirely.

misconceptions.question: Does pure water in the chemical sense mean water with nothing harmful in it?
misconceptions.correct: Pure water contains only water; a sample can be chemically pure and a sample can be safe to drink, and neither guarantees the other.
misconceptions.misconception: Pure water means water with no germs or poisons in it, so as soon as a sample is described as pure I know it is fit to drink.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students map 'pure' onto 'harmless' because both are positive words, and because the treated water they drink really is both safe and fairly clean. The word purification in Required practical 8 reinforces the link.
misconceptions.correction: Judge purity by whether anything other than water is present, and judge potability by the levels of dissolved salts and microbes. A sample of distilled water is pure; a sample of tap water is potable but not pure.

misconceptions.question: What do the filter beds in a water treatment works actually take out?
misconceptions.correct: Filter beds remove insoluble solids such as grit, leaves and suspended particles. They do not remove dissolved salts.
misconceptions.misconception: The filter beds clean the water completely - the sand traps the salts that are dissolved in it as well as the bits floating in it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture a filter as a barrier that stops everything smaller behind it, and they have often not separated 'dissolved' from 'suspended' in their minds. Filtration in the lab is taught as a way of separating a solid from a liquid, which sounds like it should catch salt too.
misconceptions.correction: Dissolved particles are single ions or molecules mixed among the water molecules, far smaller than any gap in a filter bed, so they pass straight through. That is exactly why sea water cannot be made potable by filtering, and why distillation or reverse osmosis is needed instead.

misconceptions.question: Does sterilising the water also remove the substances dissolved in it?
misconceptions.correct: Sterilising kills microbes. It has no effect on the dissolved salts, which stay in the potable water.
misconceptions.misconception: Once water has been sterilised there is nothing left in it at all, so sterilised water is pure water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sterile sounds absolute, and students merge every treatment step into one general idea of 'cleaning'. They also expect a treatment works to end with water that is as clean as possible.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the two jobs separate: filter beds deal with insoluble solids, sterilising deals with microbes, and neither deals with dissolved salts. That is why the specification says potable water still contains dissolved substances.

misconceptions.question: Does ground water need any treatment before it is drunk?
misconceptions.correct: Ground water is still treated: an appropriate source is chosen, the water is passed through filter beds, and it is sterilised.
misconceptions.misconception: Ground water has already trickled through rock, so the rock has filtered it and it is naturally safe to drink straight from the ground.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Spring water is sold as natural and untreated, and students know that rock does filter out particles, so they extend that to microbes as well.
misconceptions.correction: Rock removes insoluble particles but cannot be relied on to remove harmful microbes, so the UK sequence of choosing a source, filtering and sterilising is applied to ground water too. What ground water avoids is desalination, not treatment.

misconceptions.question: Could sea water be made potable by filtering and sterilising it, like river water?
misconceptions.correct: No. Filtering and sterilising do not remove dissolved salts, so salty water must be desalinated by distillation or a membrane process such as reverse osmosis.
misconceptions.misconception: Sea water is just dirtier water, so put it through the same filter beds and add a bit more chlorine and it will be drinkable.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat all water treatment as one process that can simply be made stronger, and they do not distinguish the type of impurity from its amount.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what has to be removed. Fresh water needs insoluble solids and microbes taken out, which filtering and sterilising do. Sea water also has a large amount of dissolved salt, and only desalination removes that.

misconceptions.question: If a country is short of fresh water, why not just desalinate sea water?
misconceptions.correct: Desalination is used where supplies of fresh water are limited, but distillation and membrane processes require large amounts of energy, which makes it expensive.
misconceptions.misconception: There is a limitless amount of sea water, so desalination is the obvious cheap answer to any water shortage.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The raw material really is free and unlimited, and students do not automatically count energy as a cost. Boiling a kettle feels cheap, so boiling sea water sounds cheap.
misconceptions.correction: Water has a high boiling point and evaporating it takes a great deal of energy; forcing water through a membrane takes a great deal of energy too. That is why the UK, which has plentiful fresh water, chooses a fresh source, filters and sterilises instead.

misconceptions.question: How does reverse osmosis separate salt from sea water?
misconceptions.correct: Reverse osmosis is a membrane process: the water is forced through a membrane that holds back the dissolved salts. It does not involve boiling.
misconceptions.misconception: Reverse osmosis is a type of distillation - the water is boiled and the steam passes through the membrane, leaving the salt behind.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both processes are met in the same sentence of the specification as ways of desalinating, and both are described as needing large amounts of energy, so students merge them.
misconceptions.correction: Distillation separates by change of state, using heat. Reverse osmosis separates by size, using pressure to push water through a membrane while the dissolved salts are held back. Both are desalination, but only distillation involves boiling.

misconceptions.question: If a resource is natural, does that make it renewable?
misconceptions.correct: No. Crude oil, natural gas and metal ores are all natural, and all finite, because they are being used far faster than they form.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that comes out of the Earth naturally will keep on being made naturally, so natural resources are renewable and only man-made things run out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word natural carries a sense of endless renewal, and students know oil formed from living things, which sounds like a process that must still be happening.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the rate of formation with the rate of use. Crude oil took millions of years to form and is being extracted in a matter of centuries, so it is finite. A replanted forest regrows in decades, so timber can be renewable.

misconceptions.question: Can a renewable resource ever run out?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. A resource is only renewable if it is replaced at least as fast as it is used, so a renewable resource used too quickly can still be exhausted.
misconceptions.misconception: Renewable means it renews itself no matter what we do, so a renewable resource is unlimited and we can use as much as we like.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Renewable is taught as the opposite of finite, and students read the opposite of 'runs out' as 'lasts for ever' rather than 'can be maintained'.
misconceptions.correction: Renewable describes a rate, not a guarantee. A forest felled faster than it is replanted disappears. This is exactly the point of sustainable development: meeting today's needs without stopping future generations meeting theirs.

misconceptions.question: Does sustainable development mean giving up finite resources altogether?
misconceptions.correct: Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
misconceptions.misconception: To be sustainable we have to stop using anything finite - no more crude oil, no more metal ores, nothing that could run out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sustainability is usually met first as an environmental slogan about cutting things out, and students see finite resources as the villain of the story rather than as something to be used carefully.
misconceptions.correction: Use the definition. Sustainable development is about meeting present needs in a way that does not deprive future generations, which includes using finite resources more efficiently, recycling them, and improving industrial processes - not abandoning them.

misconceptions.question: Is a product from a farm or a factory a synthetic product?
misconceptions.correct: Agricultural products such as wheat, cotton and wool are natural products supplemented by farming. Synthetic products are man-made substitutes such as synthetic rubber.
misconceptions.misconception: If it has been grown deliberately on a farm or processed in a factory, it counts as synthetic rather than natural.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students equate 'synthetic' with 'human involvement of any kind', and modern farming and milling look industrial, so the line between growing something and manufacturing it blurs.
misconceptions.correction: Ask where the substance itself came from. Flour is milled wheat and wool cloth is spun fleece, so both are still natural products supplemented by agriculture. Synthetic rubber is built by chemical reactions from crude oil, so it replaces a natural product with a man-made one.

misconceptions.question: Can waste water be released into a river once the solids have settled out?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sewage and agricultural waste water require removal of organic matter and harmful microbes, and industrial waste water may also require removal of harmful chemicals.
misconceptions.misconception: Once the water looks clear and the solid bits have sunk to the bottom, it is fine to let it flow into the river.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Judging water by appearance is natural, and sedimentation genuinely does make the effluent look much cleaner. Dissolved and microscopic hazards are invisible.
misconceptions.correction: Sedimentation only separates the sludge from the effluent. The effluent still contains organic matter and harmful microbes, so it goes on to aerobic biological treatment, and industrial waste water may need harmful chemicals removed as well.

misconceptions.question: Which part of sewage is treated anaerobically and which aerobically?
misconceptions.correct: Sewage sludge undergoes anaerobic digestion; the effluent undergoes aerobic biological treatment.
misconceptions.misconception: The sludge is the solid part so air can get to it easily, and the liquid effluent is the one that has no air in it - so the sludge is aerobic and the effluent anaerobic.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two stages sit side by side in the specification with similar-looking words, and students reason from a plausible but wrong picture of where air can reach.
misconceptions.correction: Learn them as a pair: sludge sinks, so it is digested without air - anaerobic digestion; effluent is the liquid that is pumped on and has air blown through it - aerobic treatment. Sludge with anaerobic, effluent with aerobic.

misconceptions.question: Does sedimentation deal with the harmful microbes in sewage?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sedimentation separates sewage sludge from effluent; the microbes are dealt with by the biological treatment that follows.
misconceptions.misconception: Letting the sewage stand kills the germs, because the harmful things sink to the bottom with the sludge and the water above is left clean.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect each stage to make the water safer in every respect, and settling is a very visible change, so it is credited with doing more than it does.
misconceptions.correction: Sedimentation is a physical separation driven by gravity; nothing is killed. Microbes remain in both the sludge and the effluent, which is why the sludge is digested anaerobically and the effluent given aerobic biological treatment.

misconceptions.question: Does screening and grit removal take out the harmful chemicals in waste water?
misconceptions.correct: No. Screening and grit removal take out large solids and grit only. Harmful chemicals in industrial waste water need a separate removal step.
misconceptions.misconception: Screening is the cleaning stage, so it takes out everything harmful, chemicals included, before the rest of the treatment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It is the first stage, and students assume the first stage is the main one. The word screening suggests something thorough, like a security check.
misconceptions.correction: Screening is a coarse physical barrier: rags, sticks and grit are caught, nothing else. Dissolved chemicals pass straight through, which is why the specification says industrial waste water may require removal of harmful chemicals as well as organic matter.

misconceptions.question: Which is easiest to turn into potable water: waste water, ground water or salt water?
misconceptions.correct: Ground water is the easiest, because it is already fresh water and needs only filtering and sterilising. Waste water and salt water both need much more treatment.
misconceptions.misconception: Waste water must be the easiest because it is fresh water already - it has just got dirty, and dirt is easy to take out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly notice that waste water is not salty, and then treat 'not salty' as 'nearly there', without weighing up the organic matter, microbes and possible harmful chemicals.
misconceptions.correction: Compare what has to be removed at each stage. Ground water needs insoluble solids and microbes removed. Waste water needs several stages of physical and biological treatment. Salt water needs energy-hungry desalination as well.

misconceptions.question: A value is 10 to the power 4 and another is 10 to the power 2. How many times bigger is the first?
misconceptions.correct: It is 100 times bigger - two orders of magnitude, because 10 to the power 4 divided by 10 to the power 2 is 10 to the power 2.
misconceptions.misconception: The powers are 4 and 2, so the first number is twice as big as the second one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students compare the indices by subtracting them and then read the answer as a multiplier instead of as a power of ten. Standard form is still being learned alongside this content.
misconceptions.correction: Subtracting the indices gives the number of orders of magnitude, not the factor. A difference of 2 in the index means a factor of 10 x 10 = 100. One order of magnitude is a factor of ten.

misconceptions.question: A sample of water has the lowest pH of a set. Does that mean it has the most dissolved solids?
misconceptions.correct: No. pH measures acidity; the mass of dissolved solids is found by evaporating a known volume and weighing the residue. They are separate measurements.
misconceptions.misconception: The more stuff there is dissolved in a water sample, the more acidic it will be, so the sample with the lowest pH must be the most concentrated one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are numbers in the same results table, and students look for a single ranking of 'how contaminated' a sample is rather than reading each measurement for what it actually reports.
misconceptions.correction: Read each column for what it measures. A sample can be neutral and full of dissolved salts, or slightly acidic and very dilute. In Required practical 8 the pH and the mass of dissolved solids are found by different methods and must be interpreted separately.

misconceptions.question: When a water sample is distilled, where is the pure water?
misconceptions.correct: The pure water is the distillate, the liquid that evaporates, condenses and is collected. The dissolved solids stay behind in the flask.
misconceptions.misconception: The dissolved solids evaporate off with the steam, so the pure water is what is left behind in the flask at the end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'left behind' with 'what we wanted to keep', as in filtration where the residue is sometimes the product, and they lose track of which component actually changes state.
misconceptions.correction: Only the water boils at the temperature used; the dissolved salts have far higher boiling points and cannot leave the flask. So the vapour is water only, and the condensed distillate is the pure water. Evaporating that distillate to dryness leaves no residue.

misconceptions.question: Are phytomining and bioleaching used because they are quicker than mining?
misconceptions.correct: They are used because copper ores are becoming scarce and these methods can extract copper from low-grade ores while avoiding digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.
misconceptions.misconception: New methods are always improvements on old ones, so phytomining and bioleaching must produce copper faster and in larger amounts than traditional mining.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume newer means better in every way, and the specification calls them 'new ways', which invites that reading. Biological processes are also rarely presented to them as slow.
misconceptions.correction: The reason given is the ore, not the speed: copper-rich ores are running out, so low-grade ores must be worked. The stated advantage is avoiding the digging, moving and disposal of huge amounts of rock. Growing and harvesting a crop is not a fast process.

misconceptions.question: After phytomining plants are burned, is there copper metal in the ash?
misconceptions.correct: The ash contains metal compounds. Those compounds still have to be processed - for example by displacement using scrap iron or by electrolysis - to obtain the metal.
misconceptions.misconception: The plants soak up copper metal and burning them leaves the copper behind, so you can just collect the copper out of the ash.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Burning is thought of as 'burning away everything else', and students rarely distinguish a metal from its compounds when the metal's name appears in both.
misconceptions.correction: Plants absorb metal compounds, not metal atoms, and burning them produces ash that contains metal compounds. The compounds are dissolved to give a solution of copper compounds, and only then is the metal obtained by displacement or electrolysis.

misconceptions.question: Do the bacteria used in bioleaching turn the ore into copper metal?
misconceptions.correct: No. The bacteria produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds, which are then processed to obtain the metal.
misconceptions.misconception: The bacteria eat the rock and leave behind lumps of copper metal, so bioleaching gives you the metal directly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word extraction makes students expect the metal itself at the end of the biological step, and living things are often imagined as doing the whole job on their own.
misconceptions.correction: Bioleaching produces a leachate solution of copper compounds. Getting the metal out of that solution needs a further chemical step: displacement using scrap iron, or electrolysis.

misconceptions.question: What does low-grade ore mean?
misconceptions.correct: A low-grade ore contains only a small percentage of the metal.
misconceptions.misconception: Low-grade ore means poor-quality rock that has been contaminated or spoiled, perhaps by pollution or by weathering.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Grade is used in everyday speech to mean quality, so low grade is read as damaged or substandard rather than as a statement about concentration.
misconceptions.correction: Grade here means the proportion of metal present. A low-grade copper ore is perfectly good rock that simply contains too little copper for traditional extraction to be worthwhile, which is why phytomining and bioleaching are being developed for it.

misconceptions.question: Why does scrap iron take copper out of a solution of a copper compound?
misconceptions.correct: Iron is more reactive than copper, so iron displaces copper from the solution: Fe + CuSO4 goes to FeSO4 + Cu.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper is the more reactive metal, so it is the copper that pushes the iron out and comes out of the solution as metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the copper appearing as a solid and read that as the copper 'winning'. Copper's familiarity and its shiny appearance also make it feel like the stronger metal.
misconceptions.correction: In a displacement reaction the more reactive metal goes into solution and the less reactive metal comes out as the element. Iron is above copper in the reactivity series, so iron enters the solution as iron sulfate and copper is deposited as the metal.

misconceptions.question: In the electrolysis of a solution of a copper compound, where does the copper appear?
misconceptions.correct: At the negative electrode, because copper ions are positively charged and are attracted to it.
misconceptions.misconception: Copper is a positive sort of thing and forms positive ions, so it must be produced at the positive electrode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students match the word positive in 'positive ion' to the word positive in 'positive electrode' rather than thinking about attraction between opposite charges.
misconceptions.correction: Opposite charges attract. Copper ions carry a positive charge, so they move to the negative electrode, gain electrons there and are deposited as copper metal.

misconceptions.question: What counts as one of the Earth's resources?
misconceptions.correct: Resources come from the Earth, the oceans and the atmosphere, and are used to provide warmth, shelter, food and transport, with natural resources supplemented by agriculture.
misconceptions.misconception: The Earth's resources means the fuels and metals that are dug out of the ground; food and timber are separate from that.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mining and drilling are the images that accompany the phrase 'the Earth's resources' in most media, and food is thought of as coming from shops or farms rather than from the Earth.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: resources provide warmth, shelter, food and transport, and they are drawn from the Earth, the oceans and the atmosphere. Timber, cotton, wool and farmed food are resources every bit as much as coal and iron ore are.

misconceptions.question: Is ultraviolet light a chemical added to drinking water?
misconceptions.correct: No. Ultraviolet light is one of the sterilising agents used for potable water, alongside chlorine and ozone, and it adds nothing to the water.
misconceptions.misconception: All three sterilising agents are substances put into the water, so ultraviolet light must be some kind of chemical that is added as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three agents are listed together in one sentence, and the word agent suggests a substance. Chlorine and ozone really are added, so students generalise from them.
misconceptions.correction: Chlorine and ozone are chemicals added to the water; ultraviolet light is radiation shone through it, which kills microbes without adding any substance. All three are sterilising agents, but only two of them are chemicals.

misconceptions.question: Do phytomining and bioleaching mean that copper supplies are no longer limited?
misconceptions.correct: No. The Earth's resources of metal ores are limited. These methods make low-grade ores usable, but they do not create more copper.
misconceptions.misconception: Now that copper can be extracted from low-grade ores, there is effectively an endless supply of copper and it will never run out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Extending a supply is easily read as removing a limit, and students are relieved to hear that a shortage has a solution.
misconceptions.correction: The total amount of copper in the Earth's crust is fixed. Phytomining and bioleaching let us reach copper we could not economically reach before, which extends the supply, but the resource is still finite - which is why recycling and sustainable development still matter.

misconceptions.question: Is potable water produced in the same way everywhere in the world?
misconceptions.correct: No. The methods used to produce potable water depend on available supplies of water and local conditions.
misconceptions.misconception: There is one correct way to make water drinkable, so every country must filter and sterilise fresh water just as the UK does.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn the UK sequence in detail and take it as the definition of water treatment rather than as one response to one country's conditions.
misconceptions.correction: The starting material decides the method. Where rain provides plentiful fresh water, a source is chosen, filtered and sterilised. Where fresh water is limited, desalination of salty water or sea water may be required instead.

misconceptions.question: If a material can be recycled, does that make it a renewable resource?
misconceptions.correct: No. Recycling makes a finite resource last longer, but the ore it originally came from is still finite.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals can be melted down and used again and again, so metals are renewable rather than finite.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Recycling is presented as the environmentally responsible option, and 'used again' sounds very like 'renewed'. The distinction between reusing existing material and forming new material is easy to miss.
misconceptions.correction: Renewable means the resource itself is being replaced as fast as it is used. No new iron ore is forming on a useful timescale, so recycling only slows the depletion of a finite resource - it does not turn it into a renewable one.

misconceptions.question: If a process uses less of a finite raw material, has the resource become renewable?
misconceptions.correct: No. Improving a process makes better use of a finite resource and supports sustainable development, but the resource remains finite.
misconceptions.misconception: If chemistry finds a way to use much less of a raw material, that material stops counting as finite because it will now last indefinitely.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students hear that improved processes help sustainability and collapse two separate ideas - using a resource well, and the resource being replaced - into one.
misconceptions.correction: Finite or renewable depends on whether the resource is being replaced, not on how carefully it is used. Using less is exactly what sustainable development asks for: meeting current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

misconceptions.question: Two values are 3.5 x 10 to the power 4 and 3.5 x 10 to the power 2. Are they about the same size?
misconceptions.correct: No. They differ by two orders of magnitude: the first is about 100 times the second.
misconceptions.misconception: Both numbers start with 3.5, so they are roughly the same - the powers of ten are just a detail about how they are written.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The eye is drawn to the leading digits, which look identical, and students who are not fluent in standard form treat the power of ten as formatting rather than as a multiplier.
misconceptions.correction: In standard form the power of ten carries almost all of the size. Write them out: 35 000 and 350. Comparing the powers first, then the leading numbers, is the reliable order of working.

misconceptions.question: Is filtered water safe to drink?
misconceptions.correct: No. Filtering removes insoluble solids; the water is only safe once it has been sterilised to kill microbes.
misconceptions.misconception: Once water has gone through the filter beds it is clear, so the germs have been taken out with everything else and it is ready to drink.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Clear water looks clean, and students know filters are used to purify things. Microbes being smaller than the gaps in a filter bed is not obvious without being told.
misconceptions.correction: Filter beds and sterilising do different jobs. The specification gives sterilising as a separate step precisely because filtering does not deal with microbes, and the sterilising agents used are chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.

misconceptions.question: Are screening, grit removal and sedimentation all doing the same job?
misconceptions.correct: No. Screening and grit removal take out large solids and grit at the start; sedimentation then lets the remaining solids settle to produce sewage sludge and effluent.
misconceptions.misconception: All three stages just take solids out of the sewage, so they are really one long stage that could be done in any order.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All three are physical separations of solids from liquid, and students group them by what they have in common instead of by what each produces.
misconceptions.correction: Track the products. Screening and grit removal produce screenings and grit that leave the process. Sedimentation produces two streams that are both treated further: sewage sludge, which is digested anaerobically, and effluent, which is treated aerobically.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about how humans use the Earth's resources is correct?

options.text: Resources provide warmth, shelter, food and transport
options.rationale: This is what the specification states: humans use the Earth's resources to provide warmth, shelter, food and transport.

options.text: Resources means the fuels and metals taken from rock
options.rationale: Mining and drilling are the images most students attach to the phrase, so they exclude food, timber and clothing from the list.

options.text: Farmed products count as synthetic rather than natural
options.rationale: Deliberate growing and industrial processing look man-made, so students reclassify agricultural products as synthetic.

options.text: Only the oceans and atmosphere are true resources
options.rationale: Picks up the oceans and atmosphere from the specification's list but drops the Earth itself, which is the largest source of all.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a natural product that has been replaced by a synthetic product?

options.text: Bread baked in a factory from farmed wheat grain
options.rationale: Factory production makes students label the product synthetic, but milled wheat is still an agricultural product.

options.text: Rubber for tyres, once made only from tree latex
options.rationale: Natural rubber tapped from trees has been largely replaced by synthetic rubber made by chemical reactions from crude oil.

options.text: Wool cloth woven from the fleece of farmed sheep
options.rationale: Processing a natural fibre feels like manufacture, but the substance itself is still a natural product supplemented by agriculture.

options.text: Timber from forests, which can never be used up
options.rationale: Students who read renewable as unlimited pick this, and it is a natural product with no synthetic replacement named here.

mcqs.stem: Where do the finite resources that are processed to provide energy and materials come from?

options.text: From rocks and mines beneath the ground only
options.rationale: Resources are pictured as things that are dug up, which leaves out the oceans and the atmosphere.

options.text: From any source that is natural and not man-made
options.rationale: Students who equate natural with finite, or natural with renewable, answer by origin rather than by the three places named.

options.text: From the Earth, the oceans and the atmosphere
options.rationale: The specification states that finite resources from the Earth, oceans and atmosphere are processed to provide energy and materials.

options.text: From the Earth and from farmed crops and animals
options.rationale: Farming is genuinely a source of resources, but it supplements natural resources rather than being one of the three places named.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the definition of sustainable development?

options.text: Stopping all use of finite resources so nothing is used up
options.rationale: Sustainability is met first as a slogan about cutting things out, so students choose the most self-denying option.

options.text: Using only renewable resources and never using any others
options.rationale: Students who believe renewable resources are unlimited see them as the only sustainable choice.

options.text: Developing new products as fast as new resources are found
options.rationale: Reads development as the main word and attaches sustainability to a steady rate of discovery rather than to future generations.

options.text: Meeting current needs without compromising future generations
options.rationale: This is the specification's own definition: development that meets the needs of current generations without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

mcqs.stem: A chemist develops a catalyst that lets a fertiliser be manufactured using less energy and less raw material. Why is this an example of the role of chemistry described in the specification?

options.text: It improves an industrial process and aids sustainable development
options.rationale: Chemistry improves agricultural and industrial processes and contributes to sustainable development, which is exactly what using less energy and less raw material achieves.

options.text: It removes the need for farming to use any finite resources
options.rationale: Students who think sustainability means eliminating finite resources read any improvement as their complete removal.

options.text: It turns a finite resource into a renewable one by using less
options.rationale: Using less feels like making a resource last for ever, but finite and renewable depend on the rate of replacement.

options.text: It proves the Earth's supply of raw materials can never run out
options.rationale: An overstatement of efficiency gains; making a process more efficient does not change the fact that the resource is finite.

mcqs.stem: Which of these resources is renewable rather than finite?

options.text: Crude oil, because it formed from living things
options.rationale: A biological origin suggests to students that the process is still going on fast enough to replace what is used.

options.text: Timber from a forest replanted after felling
options.rationale: The trees are replaced at a rate comparable with the rate of felling, so the resource can be maintained.

options.text: Iron ore, because iron can be recycled endlessly
options.rationale: Recycling reuses metal that already exists; no new ore is being formed, so the resource stays finite.

options.text: Natural gas, because more of it is found each year
options.rationale: Finding new reserves is not the same as forming new gas, and discovery cannot keep pace with use indefinitely.

mcqs.stem: Why are metal ores described as finite resources?

options.text: They can be recycled, so supplies keep growing
options.rationale: Recycling is confused with renewal, so students take it as evidence that the resource is not finite at all.

options.text: They are made by people rather than formed naturally
options.rationale: If natural is assumed to mean renewable, then finite must mean man-made, which reverses the meaning of both words.

options.text: They are used far faster than they are being formed
options.rationale: This is what finite means: the rate of use greatly exceeds the rate of formation, so supplies will run out.

options.text: They are found in only a few countries in the world
options.rationale: Uneven distribution affects supply and price, but a resource spread over every continent could still be finite.

mcqs.stem: 100 cm3 of four water samples was evaporated to dryness. The residues were: P 0.02 g, Q 0.35 g, R 1.80 g, S 3.60 g. Which conclusion does the data support?

options.text: Sample S must have the lowest pH of the four
options.rationale: Students look for one ranking of contamination and assume the most concentrated sample must also be the most acidic.

options.text: Sample P must be safe to drink as it is pure
options.rationale: A small residue is read as purity, and purity is read as safety, but the data says nothing about microbes.

options.text: Sample R is sea water as its residue is large
options.rationale: A large residue is consistent with sea water but does not identify it; the data gives masses, not sources.

options.text: Sample P contains the fewest dissolved solids
options.rationale: Equal volumes were evaporated, so the smallest residue means the smallest mass of dissolved solids.

mcqs.stem: A table gives the dissolved solids in sea water as 3.5 x 10^4 mg per dm3 and in UK tap water as 3.5 x 10^2 mg per dm3. How do the two compare?

options.text: Sea water contains about 100 times as much
options.rationale: The indices differ by 2, which is two orders of magnitude, so a factor of 10 x 10 = 100.

options.text: Sea water contains about 2 times as much
options.rationale: Subtracting the indices gives 2, which students report as the multiplier rather than as the number of orders of magnitude.

options.text: The two are about the same, as both are 3.5
options.rationale: The identical leading numbers dominate a quick reading, and the power of ten is treated as formatting.

options.text: Sea water contains about 1000 times as much
options.rationale: Comes from counting three orders of magnitude, often by miscounting the zeros written out rather than dividing the powers.

mcqs.stem: Why is potable water not pure water in the chemical sense?

options.text: It contains microbes that filtering cannot remove
options.rationale: Potable water must have sufficiently low levels of microbes, so remaining microbes are not the reason it is impure.

options.text: It still contains dissolved substances such as salts
options.rationale: The specification states that potable water is not pure water in the chemical sense because it contains dissolved substances.

options.text: It is safe to drink, so it must be chemically pure
options.rationale: Safe and pure are treated as the same idea, so students choose the option that says potable water is pure.

options.text: It is sterilised, so nothing at all is left in it
options.rationale: Sterile is read as absolute, so sterilising is credited with removing dissolved salts as well as microbes.

mcqs.stem: What must drinking water have, for humans, according to the specification?

options.text: No dissolved substances of any kind in it
options.rationale: Pure is equated with safe, so students demand the total absence of dissolved substances.

options.text: Only insoluble particles that filters remove
options.rationale: Students who think filtering handles everything reduce water quality to the removal of solids.

options.text: Low levels of dissolved salts and of microbes
options.rationale: The specification states that drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes.

options.text: Low levels of oxygen and of dissolved gases
options.rationale: Dissolved gases are a real feature of water samples, but they are not what the specification sets a limit on.

mcqs.stem: In the UK, most potable water is produced by which sequence?

options.text: Choose any source, distil it, then add back some salts
options.rationale: Students who see all treatment as one strong process assume the most thorough method is the standard one.

options.text: Choose a ground water source and use it with no treatment
options.rationale: Rock is credited with filtering the water naturally, so ground water is thought to need nothing doing to it.

options.text: Sterilise the water first, then filter it, then pick a source
options.rationale: The right three steps in an impossible order; sterilising before filtering would leave the solids in and wastes the agent.

options.text: Choose a fresh source, pass through filter beds, sterilise
options.rationale: This is the specification's sequence: choosing an appropriate source of fresh water, passing the water through filter beds, and sterilising.

mcqs.stem: Why is water passed through filter beds at a treatment works?

options.text: To remove insoluble solids such as grit and leaves
options.rationale: Filter beds are a physical barrier that traps suspended, insoluble material.

options.text: To remove the dissolved salts present in the water
options.rationale: Dissolved particles are pictured as small lumps that a fine enough filter would catch.

options.text: To kill the harmful microbes present in the water
options.rationale: Clear water looks safe, so filtering is credited with the job that sterilising actually does.

options.text: To make the water pure enough for use in a laboratory
options.rationale: Laboratory-pure water comes from distillation; filtering cannot remove anything that is dissolved.

mcqs.stem: Which set gives three sterilising agents used in producing potable water?

options.text: Chlorine, oxygen and ultraviolet light
options.rationale: Oxygen is swapped for ozone, an easy slip since ozone is an allotrope of oxygen and both are written with O.

options.text: Chlorine, ozone and ultraviolet light
options.rationale: These are the three sterilising agents the specification names for potable water.

options.text: Chlorine, ozone and a fine sand filter
options.rationale: Filtering is believed to remove microbes, so a filter is accepted as a way of sterilising.

options.text: Filtration, distillation and sedimentation
options.rationale: Sterilising is understood as general cleaning, so separation processes are offered in place of agents that kill microbes.

mcqs.stem: A water treatment works uses ultraviolet light instead of chlorine. What does this achieve?

options.text: It adds a chemical that dissolves into the water
options.rationale: All three sterilising agents are listed together, so ultraviolet light is assumed to be a substance too.

options.text: It removes the dissolved salts present in the water
options.rationale: Sterilising is credited with removing dissolved substances rather than with killing microbes.

options.text: It kills the microbes without adding any chemical
options.rationale: Ultraviolet light is radiation, so it sterilises the water without introducing any substance into it.

options.text: It filters out the insoluble solids left in the water
options.rationale: Confuses the sterilising step with the filter beds that come before it.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of processes can be used to desalinate salty water?

options.text: Filtration and sedimentation
options.rationale: Filtering is thought to catch dissolved salts, so physical separations look sufficient.

options.text: Distillation and chlorination
options.rationale: Distillation is right but chlorination sterilises rather than removing salt; the two treatment ideas are merged.

options.text: Filter beds and sterilising
options.rationale: This is the UK fresh water sequence applied to sea water, which leaves all the dissolved salt behind.

options.text: Distillation and reverse osmosis
options.rationale: The specification states that desalination can be done by distillation or by processes that use membranes such as reverse osmosis.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about desalination is correct?

options.text: It requires large amounts of energy to remove the salt
options.rationale: The specification states that distillation and membrane processes require large amounts of energy.

options.text: Passing sea water through filter beds removes the salt
options.rationale: Sea water is treated as merely dirtier water, so the fresh water steps are assumed to work on it.

options.text: It is cheap, so the UK uses it for most of its supply
options.rationale: Sea water is free and unlimited, so students do not count the energy as a cost.

options.text: It works by adding chlorine to break the salt down
options.rationale: Chlorine is remembered as a water treatment chemical and is wrongly given a salt-removing role.

mcqs.stem: How does the treatment of ground water differ from the treatment of salty water?

options.text: Salty water is given extra chlorine instead of filtering
options.rationale: More sterilising agent is offered as the answer to a stronger contaminant, but chlorine does not remove dissolved salt.

options.text: Ground water is filtered and sterilised, not desalinated
options.rationale: Ground water is fresh water, so it needs the source chosen, filter beds and sterilising; salty water must be desalinated as well.

options.text: Ground water needs no treatment at all before drinking
options.rationale: Rock is assumed to have already filtered and cleaned the water underground.

options.text: Salty water needs only filtering and sterilising as well
options.rationale: Students who think filters trap dissolved salts see no difference between the two sources.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 8, how is the mass of dissolved solids in a water sample found?

options.text: Distil the sample and weigh the liquid collected
options.rationale: The distillate is assumed to carry the dissolved solids over with the water vapour.

options.text: Weigh the solid caught in the filter paper
options.rationale: Filtering is believed to trap dissolved material, so the residue on the paper is taken as the answer.

options.text: Evaporate a known volume and weigh the residue
options.rationale: The water evaporates and the dissolved solids are left behind, so their mass can be weighed directly.

options.text: Measure the pH of the sample and convert it
options.rationale: Both are measurements made in this practical, so students assume one can be turned into the other.

mcqs.stem: A student distils a sample of sea water. Where is the pure water at the end?

options.text: In both parts, since sea water is safe once boiled
options.rationale: Safe and pure are treated as the same idea, so boiling is taken to purify the whole sample.

options.text: In the solid salt crystals left behind on heating
options.rationale: The visible product at the end of the experiment is mistaken for the target substance.

options.text: In the glass flask that the sea water was heated in
options.rationale: What is left behind is assumed to be the wanted product, as it sometimes is in filtration.

options.text: In the liquid that condenses and is collected
options.rationale: Only the water evaporates; it condenses as the distillate, which contains no dissolved solids.

mcqs.stem: Sewage and agricultural waste water require the removal of which substances before release?

options.text: Organic matter and harmful microbes
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states for sewage and agricultural waste water.

options.text: Only the solids that settle out
options.rationale: Water that looks clear after settling is judged fit to release.

options.text: Dissolved salts and dissolved oxygen
options.rationale: Imports the language of drinking water quality into a question about waste water.

options.text: Only harmful industrial chemicals
options.rationale: The requirement for industrial waste water is applied to sewage as well, dropping the organic matter and microbes.

mcqs.stem: How can the treatment needed for industrial waste water differ from that for sewage?

options.text: Only screening and grit removal are needed
options.rationale: The first stage is assumed to be the thorough one that deals with chemicals as well.

options.text: Harmful chemicals may also need removing
options.rationale: The specification states that industrial waste water may require removal of organic matter and harmful chemicals.

options.text: It can be released once it looks clean
options.rationale: Appearance is used as the test, and dissolved chemicals are invisible.

options.text: Organic matter never needs removing
options.rationale: Overstates the difference: industrial waste water may require removal of organic matter as well as harmful chemicals.

mcqs.stem: What is achieved by screening and grit removal at the start of sewage treatment?

options.text: The harmful chemicals dissolved in it are removed
options.rationale: Being the first stage, it is assumed to be the main cleaning step that handles everything.

options.text: The harmful microbes in the sewage are all killed
options.rationale: Each stage is expected to make the water safer in every respect, including biologically.

options.text: Large solid objects and grit are taken out of it
options.rationale: Screening and grit removal are a coarse physical separation of large solids and grit.

options.text: The sludge is separated from the liquid effluent
options.rationale: All the solid-removal stages are treated as one, so sedimentation's job is credited to screening.

mcqs.stem: What two things does sedimentation of sewage produce?

options.text: Sterile water and harmless dissolved gases
options.rationale: Settling is credited with killing microbes, so its product is imagined as safe water.

options.text: Grit, screened rags and other large solids
options.rationale: Sedimentation is merged with screening and grit removal, so their products are given instead.

options.text: Potable drinking water and dried sludge
options.rationale: Students who think waste water is easily made drinkable expect potable water at this stage.

options.text: Sewage sludge and liquid effluent
options.rationale: The solids settle to form sewage sludge and the liquid above it is the effluent, and each is then treated separately.

mcqs.stem: Which pairing of sewage treatment stages is correct?

options.text: Anaerobic digestion of sludge, aerobic treatment of effluent
options.rationale: This is the specification's pairing: anaerobic digestion of sewage sludge and aerobic biological treatment of effluent.

options.text: Aerobic digestion of sludge, anaerobic treatment of effluent
options.rationale: Students reason that air reaches solid sludge easily and cannot reach liquid, so they swap the two.

options.text: Anaerobic digestion of both the sludge and the effluent
options.rationale: The later stages are collapsed into one treatment applied to everything that leaves sedimentation.

options.text: Aerobic treatment of the sludge and also of the effluent
options.rationale: One familiar word is applied to both streams, which loses the distinction the specification draws.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the relative ease of obtaining potable water is correct?

options.text: Salt water is as easy to treat as ground water
options.rationale: If filtering is thought to remove dissolved salt, the two sources look equally straightforward.

options.text: Ground water is easier to treat than salt water
options.rationale: Ground water is already fresh water and needs only filtering and sterilising, while salt water needs energy-hungry desalination.

options.text: Waste water is the easiest of the three to treat
options.rationale: Waste water is not salty, which students take to mean it is nearly potable already.

options.text: Ground water needs no treatment before drinking
options.rationale: The rock is assumed to have filtered and sterilised the water underground.

mcqs.stem: Why are phytomining and bioleaching being developed as ways of obtaining copper?

options.text: They produce copper faster than traditional mining
options.rationale: Newer methods are assumed to be better in every way, including speed.

options.text: Low-grade ore is rock that has been contaminated
options.rationale: Grade is read as quality, so low-grade ore sounds like spoiled or polluted rock.

options.text: Copper ores are scarce, so low-grade ores are used
options.rationale: The specification states that copper ores are becoming scarce and these are new ways of extracting copper from low-grade ores.

options.text: Copper cannot be extracted from any ore by heating
options.rationale: Traditional smelting is assumed to have failed, rather than to have run short of suitable ore.

mcqs.stem: What advantage do phytomining and bioleaching have over traditional mining?

options.text: They produce copper in a much shorter time
options.rationale: Speed is assumed to be the advantage of any new method.

options.text: They mean copper supplies are now unlimited
options.rationale: Extending a supply is read as removing the limit on it altogether.

options.text: They give the metal with no further processing
options.rationale: Ash and leachate are assumed to contain the metal itself rather than its compounds.

options.text: They avoid moving huge amounts of waste rock
options.rationale: The specification states that these methods avoid traditional mining methods of digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.

mcqs.stem: Which sequence describes phytomining correctly?

options.text: Plants absorb metal compounds, are harvested and burned
options.rationale: This is the specification's description: plants absorb metal compounds, then are harvested and burned to produce ash containing metal compounds.

options.text: Plants absorb copper metal, which is picked out of ash
options.rationale: Burning is thought to remove everything except the metal, so the ash is imagined to contain copper itself.

options.text: Bacteria in the soil turn the ore into pure copper metal
options.rationale: The two biological methods are confused, and the biological step is credited with producing the metal.

options.text: Plants are burned to ash and then grown again in that ash
options.rationale: The right steps in an impossible order; plants must absorb the metal compounds before being harvested.

mcqs.stem: What do the bacteria used in bioleaching produce?

options.text: Heat that separates the metal from its ore
options.rationale: Extraction is associated with smelting, so a heat-producing role is invented for the bacteria.

options.text: Leachate solutions containing metal compounds
options.rationale: The specification states that bioleaching uses bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.

options.text: Pure copper metal deposited on the ore
options.rationale: The bacteria are imagined to do the whole extraction and leave the metal behind.

options.text: Ash that contains solid copper compounds
options.rationale: The product of phytomining is attributed to bioleaching, since both are biological methods.

mcqs.stem: Copper compounds in solution can be processed to obtain copper metal. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Scrap iron works because copper is more reactive
options.rationale: The copper appears as a solid, which students read as the copper winning the competition.

options.text: Electrolysis works only if the solution is heated
options.rationale: Heat is associated with metal extraction generally and is wrongly made a condition for electrolysis.

options.text: Scrap iron displaces copper as iron is more reactive
options.rationale: Iron is above copper in the reactivity series, so it displaces it: Fe + CuSO4 goes to FeSO4 + Cu.

options.text: In electrolysis copper forms at the positive electrode
options.rationale: The word positive in positive ion is matched to the positive electrode instead of applying attraction of opposite charges.

mcqs.stem: For one low-grade ore, phytomining yields 0.8 tonnes of copper per hectare each year and uses little energy; open-cast mining yields 40 tonnes per hectare each year but moves 4000 tonnes of waste rock. Which evaluation does this information support?

options.text: Phytomining is the faster method and also the cleaner one
options.rationale: New methods are assumed to win on every measure, so the yield figures are not read.

options.text: Mining can stop being used as copper supplies are endless
options.rationale: An alternative method is taken as proof that the resource is no longer limited.

options.text: Mining is the better method as its yield per year is higher
options.rationale: Reads one column only; the 4000 tonnes of waste rock per hectare is ignored entirely.

options.text: Phytomining is far slower but creates much less waste rock
options.rationale: Uses both figures: 0.8 against 40 tonnes shows the much lower yield, while avoiding 4000 tonnes of waste rock is the stated benefit.
